title: Identifying Knowledge Editing Types in Large Language Models

problem.claim: Malicious knowledge edits can cause large language models to generate toxic content and mislead users into inappropriate actions.

gap.claim: Effective measures for preventing malicious misuse of knowledge editing are lacking.

contributions.claim: The paper introduces Knowledge Editing Type Identification, a task for identifying different types of edits in large language models.
KETIBench contains five types of harmful edits and one benign factual edit.
The paper develops five classical classification models and three BERT-based models as baseline identifiers for open-source and closed-source large language models.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across 92 trials involving four models and three knowledge editing methods, all eight baseline identifiers achieved decent identification performance.
The authors report that identifier performance is independent of the reliability of the knowledge editing methods.
The authors report cross-domain generalization, including identification of edits from unknown sources.

narrative_sequence.summary: Knowledge editing is presented as an efficient technique for updating large language models.
The abstract identifies a lack of safeguards against malicious edits that can produce toxic content and mislead users.
The paper introduces the KETI task and the KETIBench benchmark for identifying harmful and benign edit types.
Eight baseline identifiers are evaluated across models and editing methods, with reported feasibility and cross-domain generalization.

source_observation.claim: The task identifies edit types rather than only evaluating the resulting model behavior.

interpretation.claim: Classifying modification types can provide an early-warning layer for detecting illicit model changes.

application.claim: Use edit-type identification as a monitoring component when deploying knowledge-edited language models.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish effectiveness beyond the reported trials or specify operational deployment conditions.

unknowns: The specific five harmful edit types and their data composition are not described.
Metrics, baseline implementation details, and comparative results are not provided.
The abstract does not report limitations, error cases, or independent verification.
